questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About Orthogonal Vectors in Inner Product Spaces
questions.problem:
Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Given the functions $f(t)=t$ and $g(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ which of the following statements are true?

- $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=2\pi $
- $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=0$
- $f(t)⊥g(t)$ with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to evaluate 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡t & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-\pi }^{\pi }-{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{-\pi }^{\pi }+{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi ))+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =(\pi +\pi )+(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now examine the statements:

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. This is as a result of the above calculations.

- Statement III is false. Since the inner product is not zero, our vectors are not orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Components of Orthogonal Vectors in Inner Product Spaces of Polynomials
questions.problem:
Let $V={R}_{2}[t]$ be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most $2,$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=x(-2)y(-2)+x(0)y(0)+x(2)y(2).
$$

If $p(t)=1-2t$ and $q(t)=2-k{t}^{2}$ are orthogonal with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V,$ then $k=$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $p(t)$ and $q(t)$ are orthogonal, their inner product must be zero.

First, we compute the inner product using our definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨p(t),q(t)⟩ & =p(-2)q(-2)+p(0)q(0)+p(2)q(2) \\  & =(1+4)(2-4k)+(1)(2)+(1-4)(2-4k) \\  & =(10-20k)+2+(-6+12k) \\  & =6-8k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set $⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=0$ and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨p(t),q(t)⟩ & =0 \\ 6-8k & =0 \\ 8k & =6 \\ k & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Components of Orthogonal Vectors in Inner Product Spaces of Continuous Functions
questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,1],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

If $x(t)={t}^{2}$ and $y(t)=k+3t$ are orthogonal with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V,$ then $k=$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ are orthogonal, their inner product must be zero.

First, we compute the inner product using our definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x(t),y(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}(k+3t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(k{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{k{t}^{3}}{3}+\frac{3{t}^{4}}{4}){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{k}{3}+\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set $⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=0$ and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x(t),y(t)⟩ & =0 \\ \frac{k}{3}+\frac{3}{4} & =0 \\ \frac{k}{3} & =-\frac{3}{4} \\ k & =-\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Given the functions $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ and $g(t)=1,$ which of the following statements are true?

- $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=\pi $
- $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=0$
- $f(t)⊥g(t)$ with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to evaluate

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can evaluate this integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t & ={[-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}{2}|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi )}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now examine the statements:

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. This is as a result of the above calculations.

- Statement III is true. Since the inner product is zero, our vectors must be orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

$$

If $p(t)=1+{t}^{2}$ and $q(t)=-5{t}^{2}+2t+k$ are orthogonal with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V,$ then $k=$

Since $p(t)$ and $q(t)$ are orthogonal, their inner product must be zero.

First, we compute the inner product using our definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨p(t),q(t)⟩ & =p(-1)q(-1)+p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1) \\  & =(2)(k-7)+(1)(k)+(2)(k-3) \\  & =2k-14+k+2k-6 \\  & =5k-20\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set $⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=0$ and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨p(t),q(t)⟩ & =0 \\ 5k-20 & =0 \\ 5k & =20 \\ k & =4\end{aligned}
$$
